source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Start insulin immediately without potassium replacement because potassium will rise once hyperglycemia improves.","B":"Give a potassium-wasting diuretic before insulin because reducing total body potassium improves DKA treatment.","C":"Withhold fluids, potassium, and insulin until glucose falls below 250 mg/dL without treatment.","D":"Begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until the potassium level rises above 3.5 mmol/L."}}
source_row.rationale: Current consensus guidance recommends potassium replacement when admission potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L and delaying insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L. Option D is correct because insulin would shift potassium intracellularly and can worsen severe hypokalemia. A, B, and C increase risk or delay needed therapy.
source_row.source_detail: Potassium management in DKA: if potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, begin potassium replacement and delay insulin until potassium rises above 3.5 mmol/L because insulin can worsen hypokalemia and precipitate arrhythmia/respiratory muscle weakness. 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; remains current and live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has a serum potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L before insulin is started. Which sequence is expected?
